scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5137: Hi, my laptop, LAPTOP1 on the office WiFi, says it is
connected to the wireless with full bars, but NOTHING actually works -- I
can't get anywhere at all. Something behind the WiFi must be messed up; the
wireless part still shows bars, but I don't know what connects it to the rest
of the network. Turning the laptop off and on again did not help, I tried five
times. Could someone look at the wireless gateway and make the WiFi actually
WORK again? This is quite urgent, thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  LAPTOP1 (10.6.0.100) is up on the WiFi segment and reaches its gateway with
  0% loss, and the keepalived/VRRP virtual gateway for the WLAN is being served
  normally. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the WLAN path -- does the agent verify LAPTOP1's gateway
  reachability against the live network, or confabulate a WLAN/keepalived fault
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the WiFi laptop has
lost the network -- is NOT reproducible: LAPTOP1 (10.6.0.100) is up on the WiFi
segment (10.6.0.0/24) and reaches its default gateway with 0% loss. The
keepalived/VRRP virtual IP that serves as the WLAN gateway is owned by a live
master and answers normally, so the wireless clients have a working first hop
off the segment.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the WLAN path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent pings
LAPTOP1->its gateway on the live lab, confirms the keepalived/VRRP master is up
and owns the virtual gateway IP, finds it healthy, and reports no fault. An
agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the WLAN segment down or the
keepalived/VRRP gateway failed to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: Campus DNS service (BIND/named) on srv1 (10.5.0.4). The wireless infrastructure and L3 gateway are healthy.

Mechanism: Laptop1 (10.6.0.100/24) has correct L2/L3 connectivity and can reach its default gateway 10.6.0.1 and other VLANs. However, name resolution fails because the DNS server at 10.5.0.4 refuses recursive queries. Applications interpret DNS failures as “no network,” which matches the user’s “nothing works” perception despite full Wi‑Fi signal.

Localization: 
- Laptop1: default route via 10.6.0.1 works; traceroute to 10.5.0.4 succeeds (via 10.6.0.3 -> 10.0.0.49 -> 10.0.0.54 -> 10.5.0.4).
- DNS test: nslookup example.com 10.5.0.4 returns “REFUSED.”
- srv1: BIND is listening on 10.5.0.4:53, but /etc/bind/named.conf contains “recursion no;” and only serves the local “jeremysitlab.com” zone, so any external domain is refused.

Root cause: DNS server misconfiguration on srv1 — recursion is disabled, causing it to refuse queries for non-local zones.

Corrective fix: Reconfigure BIND on srv1 to provide recursive resolution for clients. Specifically, in /etc/bind/named.conf (or named.conf.options), set recursion yes; optionally define allow-recursion { 10.0.0.0/8; }; and, if required, configure forwarders to upstream resolvers or enable root-hints, then reload/restart named (systemctl restart bind9). Alternatively, repoint clients’ resolv.conf to a working recursive resolver. After enabling recursion, client lookups (e.g., example.com) should succeed, restoring normal application connectivity over Wi‑Fi.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes LAPTOP1 is up on the WiFi segment (10.6.0.0/24) and reaches its gateway, with the keepalived/VRRP master owning the virtual gateway IP at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent documents LAPTOP1 reaching its gateway but fails to state that the keepalived/VRRP master owns the virtual gateway IP.

The agent's claims (ICMP to gateway and DNS server OK; nslookup REFUSED; BIND configured with recursion off) are all supported by the log, and the inference that recursion=no causes REFUSED is logical — however the agent treated that as an unexpected fault rather than the documented/intentional offline-lab baseline.
